tldr: By exploiting the property that the Hamiltonian is maximized at the vertices of the input space in control-affine systems, the authors proposed a method to learn non-conservative neural control barrier functions (CBFs) using fast tree search to generate high-quality supervision data.
hero_caption: Comparison of learned safe sets across different methods on the inverted pendulum. Physics loss alone (PDE-only) collapses to an empty safe set, and MPC sampling over the full control domain (FCD) is overly conservative. In contrast, the proposed VRCD (right) captures the true maximal safe set (yellow boundary) almost perfectly.
overview:
Control barrier function (CBF)-based safety filters have drawn significant attention as a theoretical framework for autonomous mobile robots and drones to safely navigate around obstacles. However, manually designing closed-form CBFs that capture the theoretical "maximal safe set" while accounting for actuator limits (input constraints) is extremely difficult. Recently, approximating the value function from Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis using neural networks has become popular. Yet, there has been a dilemma: training with PDE (partial differential equation) physics losses alone tends to fall into meaningless trivial constant solutions, while generating supervision data via trajectory optimization is computationally too heavy to scale.

To address this, the authors focus on the structure commonly found in robotics: "control-affine dynamics" with "convex polytope input constraints." In this setting, the maximum value of the Hamiltonian that governs safety is always achieved at the vertices of the input polytope. That means there is no need to search the continuous input space exhaustively. Performing a discrete tree search that picks only extreme vertices enables ultra-fast, highly accurate generation of finite-horizon safety labels via GPU parallelization.

Evaluated on 15 diverse dynamical system simulations, the proposed method, "VertexCBF," reliably recovers large and accurate safe sets even where baselines fail or become overly conservative. Furthermore, the authors demonstrated high practical utility through hardware experiments where an autonomous delivery robot equipped with onboard LiDAR and a camera smoothly avoided pedestrians in a real-world environment.
contributions: Proposed a vertex-restricted tree search method that generates supervision data via GPU parallelization at high speed, exploiting the property that Hamiltonian maximization occurs at vertices under control-affine dynamics and convex polytope input constraints.

Constructed a training framework combining physics-informed HJB variational inequality loss with sparse vertex search data, alongside a residual architecture bounded above by the constraint function to prevent over-expansion of the safe set.
Demonstrated substantially higher effective safe volume and reliability over baseline methods across 15 dynamical system benchmarks with varying dimensions and constraints.
Implemented the method as an online CBF-QP filter on a real-world delivery robot, demonstrating safe avoidance of moving pedestrians in hardware experiments.

sections.heading: Why Searching Control "Vertices" Unlocks Safe Robot Control
sections.summary: Automated CBF design that guarantees safety for robots is notoriously difficult in the presence of input constraints. To learn optimal safe sets based on HJ reachability with neural CBFs, this paper proposes "VertexCBF," a new method combining fast vertex-restricted search over control polytopes with physics losses.
sections.details:
In recent years, autonomous robots have rapidly expanded into real-world applications, making safety guarantees the most critical challenge for systems operating in physical contact with their environments. A leading framework to achieve this is safety filtering, which minimally modifies nominal control inputs in real time to preserve safety. In particular, quadratic programming with control barrier functions (CBF-QP) is widely used due to its lightweight computation and high interpretability.

However, when input constraints such as motor torque limits exist alongside state constraints, handcrafting a suitable CBF is remarkably difficult. Practitioners have been forced to compromise between underestimating the safe region and sacrificing performance, or failing to avoid obstacles near boundaries due to control saturation.

Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis can theoretically derive the maximal safe set, but solving its PDE in real time is impossible. While attempts have been made to approximate this value function with neural networks, training with physics losses alone easily falls into local minima, and relying on external data leads to combinatorial explosion in sampling costs.

This is where the authors made their key insight. Under the combination of control-affine dynamics (linear in control) and convex polytope control sets—standard assumptions in CBF-QP—the control input that maximizes the Hamiltonian always lies at the vertices of the polytope. Consequently, there is no need to wander inside the continuous input space. Performing a finite-horizon tree search that only switches among vertices enables GPU-parallel generation of ground-truth labels with overwhelming efficiency.

sections.heading: Pitfalls of Physics Loss and Limitations of Prior Work
sections.summary: Prior neural CBF methods have struggled with collapsing to trivial solutions when using PDE losses alone, or with heavy computational costs when generating data via MPC sampling. This method targets the stationary HJB equation, eliminating the need for curriculum learning or heavy trajectory optimization.
sections.details:
Many prior studies have explored machine learning to obtain CBFs. Early efforts relied on SVMs or shallow neural networks, and more recently, distance-based CBFs using Gaussian Splatting have been proposed. However, these often break down in high-relative-degree systems or under input saturation.

Deep learning approaches to solve HJ reachability for maximal safe sets (such as DeepReach) have also emerged. Yet, they require delicate curriculum learning schedules to handle boundary conditions and time-evolution, making training prone to instability.

Other attempts train neural CBFs solely on physics losses from the stationary Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman variational inequality (HJB-VI). However, this variational inequality has a problematic property: any constant less than or equal to the constraint function trivially satisfies the equation. As a result, optimization easily collapses to a meaningless constant function, yielding an empty safe set.

Recent related work pairs PDE losses with supervised trajectory data collected via MPPI (sampling-based MPC). But because it addresses a time-dependent problem, curriculum learning and pre-training remain indispensable. Above all, sampling the entire input space with MPC is computationally expensive and frequently samples sub-optimal inputs. In contrast, this paper tackles the stationary formulation to eliminate the time variable and leverages the structural property of vertex control, obtaining high-quality supervision without pre-training.

sections.heading: Mathematical Formulation: Safety Definitions and CBF-QP
sections.summary: Under control-affine dynamics and convex polytope inputs, the infinite-horizon safety value function and maximal safe set are defined. This paper aims to approximate this value function as a smooth CBF and guarantee forward invariance via a CBF-QP filter.
sections.details:
This paper considers standard control-affine systems in robotics:
$\dot{x} = f(x) + g(x)u$
where state $x \in \mathcal{X}$, control input $u \in \mathcal{U}$, and the control set $\mathcal{U}$ is a compact convex polytope. The vertex set of the polytope is denoted as $\mathcal{V} = \operatorname{vert}(\mathcal{U})$. The constraint set the system must satisfy is defined using a continuous constraint function $c(x)$ as $\mathcal{C} = \{x \mid c(x) \ge 0\}$.

The infinite-horizon safety value function $V(x)$, representing the maximum of the worst-case constraint value maintainable from initial state $x$, is defined as:
$V(x) = \sup_{u(\cdot)} \inf_{t \ge 0} c(x(t))$
The set where this value function is non-negative, $\mathcal{S} = \{x \mid V(x) \ge 0\}$, is the largest set that can be kept safe by control inputs—the maximal safe set.

At runtime, a nominal control input $u_{\mathrm{nom}}$ is passed through the following quadratic program (CBF-QP) using the learned CBF $h(x) \approx V(x)$:
$u^* = \arg\min_{u \in \mathcal{U}} \|u - u_{\mathrm{nom}}\|^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad L_f h(x) + L_g h(x)u + \alpha(h(x)) \ge 0$
where $L_f, L_g$ are Lie derivatives and $\alpha$ is an extended class $\mathcal{K}$ function. As long as this QP is feasible, Nagumo's theorem ensures that the 0-superlevel set $\mathcal{S}_h = \{x \mid h(x) \ge 0\}$ is forward invariant, meaning the robot will never leave the safe set.

sections.heading: VertexCBF Architecture: Vertex-Restricted Tree Search meets Residual Networks
sections.summary: Exploiting the fact that the Hamiltonian is maximized at polytope vertices, time-discretized vertex-restricted tree search (such as beam search) generates supervision data in parallel. The neural network uses a residual architecture bounded above by the constraint function and trains on both PDE and data losses.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Time Discretization of the Vertex-Restricted Problem
In the stationary HJB variational inequality satisfied by the safety value function $V(x)$, the Hamiltonian $\max_{u \in \mathcal{U}} [\nabla V(x) (f(x) + g(x)u)]$ appears. Because the second term is purely linear in $u$ and $\mathcal{U}$ is a convex polytope, the maximum is always achieved at one of the vertices $v \in \mathcal{V}$. The authors restrict the continuous-time Hamiltonian to the vertex set $\mathcal{V}$ and discretize it using forward Euler integration with step size $\Delta t$. Rather than solving a discrete-time Bellman equation directly over all controls, restricting to vertices in continuous time before applying Euler discretization theoretically guarantees first-order local consistency with the continuous HJB-VI (Appendix A).

### 4.2 Finite-Horizon Search with Vertex-Restricted Control
Because searching over an infinite horizon is intractable, the problem is truncated to a finite horizon of length $K$. Limiting candidate inputs strictly to vertices (total count $M = |\mathcal{V}|$) forms a tree search with branching factor $M$ and depth $K$. For low-dimensional systems, exhaustive search is possible, but for larger scales, beam search (BS) with beam width $B$, stochastic beam search (SBS), or branch-and-bound (BnB) is used. Trajectory evaluations and pruning are executed in batched parallel on GPUs at very high speed. The value $V_{\Delta t}^{K,B}(x)$ obtained by beam search provides an under-approximation (conservative bound) of the true vertex search optimum, yielding safe supervision data that does not overestimate safety.

### 4.3 Network Architecture and Loss Formulation
Rather than predicting values directly, the neural network $V_\Theta(x)$ is designed using a non-negative residual $r_\Theta(x)$ relative to the constraint function $c(x)$:
$V_\Theta(x) = c(x) - r_\Theta(x)$
By applying a Softplus function to the output layer of $r_\Theta$ to make it strictly non-negative, $V_\Theta(x) \le c(x)$ is structurally guaranteed 100% of the time. This eliminates any risk of the learned safe set ballooning beyond the original hard constraint $\mathcal{C}$. Furthermore, this residual formulation prevents the network from collapsing into trivial constant solutions where the PDE loss becomes zero.

The training loss is a weighted sum (weight $\lambda$) of a physics loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PDE}}$, which penalizes violations of the stationary HJB-VI over states sampled uniformly from space, and a data loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{data}}$, representing the squared error against vertex tree-search labels. The PDE loss provides local consistency across the state space, while the data loss anchors the solution to the true maximal safe set.

sections.heading: Outstanding Performance Across 15 Dynamical Systems and Real Robot Experiments
sections.summary: Evaluated across 15 simulation environments, the method achieved the highest effective safe volume while keeping false safety low compared to physics-only (PDE-only) and MPC data (FCD). In pedestrian avoidance experiments on a real delivery robot, it achieved zero collisions across all 10 trials.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Metrics
To evaluate the proposed method, the authors tested it on 15 diverse dynamical systems, including a double integrator, inverted pendulum, kinematic car, cart-pole, and a 6-DOF underwater robot (13 state dimensions, 6 control dimensions). VertexCBF was compared against a physics-only baseline without data (PDE-only / ND) and a baseline using full-control-domain MPPI sampling (FCD), inspired by prior work. Autonomous control rollouts using the learned CBF were evaluated on three metrics:
- False Safety Rate ($\rho_{\mathrm{FS}}$): The ratio of states predicted safe that actually violated constraints (reliability metric; lower is better).
- False Unsafe Rate ($\rho_{\mathrm{FU}}$): The ratio of safe states falsely marked as unsafe (conservativeness metric).
- Effective Safe Volume ($\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}$): The fraction of state space verified safe both in prediction and rollout (practical operational volume; higher is better).

### Simulation Findings
The results were compelling. While PDE-only worked on simple systems, on moderately complex ones it repeatedly collapsed to constant solutions with an empty safe set ($\eta_{\mathrm{eff}}=0$). FCD (MPPI) recovered some safe regions, but because it predominantly sampled the interior of the control space, it missed true optimal vertex controls, remaining overly conservative with low effective volume. In contrast, the proposed VRCD (VertexCBF) achieved the lowest false safety rate and the highest (or tied-highest) effective safe volume in almost all environments. On the inverted pendulum, it nearly perfectly reconstructed the true maximal safe set (Figure F2).

### 5.1 Hardware Experiments
To verify real-time performance, the authors conducted hardware tests on a wheeled delivery robot equipped with a 3D LiDAR and stereo camera. The robot navigated toward goals using MPC while correcting its control inputs via a CBF-QP filter based on relative dynamics to detected pedestrians. In 10 trials where 1 to 2 pedestrians deliberately blocked its path, the robot performed smooth avoidance behaviors without a single collision (Figure F3). By slightly inflating the obstacle radius by just 5 cm during training to handle wheel slip and perception latency, real-world safety was fully maintained even when CBF values briefly dipped slightly negative.

captions.F2: CBF estimation results across methods on the inverted pendulum. PDE-only degenerates to a constant solution, and FCD using MPPI data is overly conservative. VRCD using vertex search captures a predicted boundary (blue dashed line) extremely close to the true safe boundary (yellow line).
captions.F3: Hardware pedestrian avoidance experiment on the delivery robot. The left plot shows the trajectory of the robot (grey) smoothly avoiding pedestrians (red boxes) toward the goal, while the right plot shows the time history of CBF values and filter-modified control inputs (dotted lines).

sections.heading: Conclusions, Future Directions, and Limitations
sections.summary: VertexCBF successfully learns accurate neural CBFs by combining high-quality supervision data with physics loss, capitalizing on the geometric properties of control-affine systems. Deriving formal error bounds and scaling to high-dimensional whole-body humanoid robots remain key future challenges.
sections.details:
### Conclusion
This paper proposed VertexCBF, a systematic learning framework for neural CBFs that approximate the stationary HJ safety value function. By focusing on control-affine dynamics and convex polytope control sets—ubiquitous structures in robotics—and leveraging the property that the Hamiltonian achieves its maximum at vertices, the method realizes fast GPU-parallel tree search without grid-based solvers or heavy continuous sampling. Combined with residual networks that strictly enforce constraint boundaries, it was demonstrated across 15 systems and real-world experiments to learn highly reliable, non-conservative safe sets.

### Limitations
The authors also explicitly discuss several limitations:
- Lack of Formal Guarantees: Because of time discretization, finite-horizon truncation, beam search approximations, and neural network representation errors, deterministic safety error bounds on the learned result are currently not guaranteed, leaving verification dependent on empirical rollouts. Integrating probabilistic guarantees like conformal prediction is an avenue for future work.
- Scalability to Vertex Explosion: As input dimensionality grows, the number of polytope vertices $M$ increases exponentially. While this work handled up to 6 control inputs (64 vertices) efficiently, applying it directly to whole-body dynamics of humanoid robots with dozens of DOFs is computationally intractable. Applying the method to reduced-order models offers a realistic path forward for such complex systems.

sections.heading: Appendix: Theoretical Proofs and Hyperparameter Insights
sections.summary: The appendix provides mathematical proofs of first-order local consistency of the discretization, details three beam search variants, and conducts ablations on the effects of step size and residual architecture on accuracy.
sections.details:
### Theoretical Foundations and Tree Search Algorithms (Appendix A, B)
In Appendix A, Taylor expansions using smooth test functions $\psi$ show that the one-step local truncation error of the vertex-restricted Euler operator is $O(\Delta t^2)$, and the finite-difference approximation error of the Hamiltonian is $O(\Delta t)$, confirming first-order local consistency with the continuous-time HJB-VI. Appendix B details GPU-batch implementations of standard beam search (BS), stochastic beam search (SBS) to prevent premature convergence to local optima, and multi-pass branch-and-bound (BnB).

### Importance of Step Size and Residual Architecture (Appendix D, E, H)
Investigating search step size $\Delta t$ on a 6-DOF underwater robot (Appendix D, Figure F6) revealed that if $\Delta t$ is too small, the prediction horizon $K\Delta t$ is too short to capture stopping distances, degrading the false safety rate. Conversely, if $\Delta t$ is too large, discretization error shrinks the safe region. Selecting an appropriate $\Delta t$ (0.1 s in this experiment) yields highly robust performance.

Furthermore, ablation experiments without the residual architecture $V_\Theta = c - r_\Theta$ using standard MLPs (Appendix E) caused PDE-only to collapse into empty safe sets in 14 out of 15 systems, highlighting how critical the residual structure is for preventing trivial solutions. Finally, Appendix H shares practical implementation details, including the onboard perception pipeline interface (Figure F8) and slack variable usage to maintain QP feasibility.

captions.F6: Comparison of search time step $\Delta t$ on the 6-DOF underwater robot. With $\Delta t=0.02$ s, the horizon is too short to detect danger, and with $\Delta t=0.4$ s, discretization error shrinks the safe region, whereas values between 0.05 s and 0.2 s yield very stable CBF boundaries.
captions.F8: Onboard PC screen on the delivery robot during hardware experiments. Camera view (top-left), 2D slice map of the neural CBF over position coordinates (bottom-left), and LiDAR point cloud pedestrian tracking (right) are integrated and processed in real time.

takeaways: By leveraging control-affine dynamics and convex input sets, continuous optimal control search can be dramatically simplified into discrete tree search over vertices only.

Physics-informed losses (PINN/HJB-VI) alone easily collapse into trivial constant solutions; pairing a residual architecture bounded by the constraint function with sparse, high-quality data anchors is exceptionally effective.
When exhaustive search is impossible in higher dimensions and longer horizons, GPU-parallel beam search can rapidly generate safe, conservative lower-bound supervision labels.
Sim-to-real gaps can be practically managed through classical safety margin engineering, such as inflating obstacle radii by a few centimeters during training.
limitations: Deterministic safety guarantees and formal error bounds covering time discretization and neural network approximation errors have not yet been established.
The number of vertices grows exponentially with actuator count, imposing computational limits on direct application to high-DOF systems like whole-body humanoids.
The setup relies on simplified relative dynamics (e.g., constant obstacle velocity), offering limited validation under sudden pedestrian accelerations or high dynamic uncertainty.
